title: The effects of changes to the built environment on the mental health and well-being of adults: Systematic review
authors: Moore, T., Kesten, J., Lopez-Lopez, J. A., McAleenan, A., Ijaz, S., Richards, A., Gray, S., Savović, J., & Audrey, S. (2018)
review_question: To assess the evidence of changes to the built environment on mental health, well-being, quality of life, social inclusion and fear of crime in adults living in urban environments in high income countries.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Included: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), cluster RCTs, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series, and regression discontinuity studies assessing physical changes to the built environment. Outcomes: mental health, well-being, quality of life, social inclusion/isolation, social capital, fear of crime. Participants: adults in urban environments in high-income countries. Excluded: studies in rural/low-middle-income countries, street lighting/CCTV, non-public realm interventions, relocation/housing refurbishment as sole intervention.

findings.consequent: Proportion with poor mental health (GHQ-12 or MHI-5)
findings.quote: The overall effect was reduced to SDID -0.03 (95% CI -0.08 to 0.02).
weak evidence of a small beneficial effect of the intervention was identified (SDID -0.13, 95% CI -0.26 to -0.01).

findings.antecedent: Urban regeneration (New Deal for Communities, Wythenshawe regeneration)
findings.quote: Pooled data from 'NDC' and 'Wythenshawe Regeneration' showed no effect on symptoms of mental health SDID -0.01 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.04).
Results from the 'Well London' RCT, suggested no differences in mental health between intervened and non-intervened areas (SDID -0.01, 95% CI -0.15 to 0.12).

findings.antecedent: Improving green infrastructure ('Greening vacant lots', 'GSW Philadelphia')
findings.quote: There was no effect of improving green infrastructure on mental health measured as stress in a single-item health question in 'Greening vacant lots' and 'GSW Philadelphia' studies.
They report improved mental health in the active commuting group, however this effect attenuated when controlled for baseline mental health (SDID 0.06, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.18).

findings.antecedent: Transport infrastructure (Road bypass for noise reduction)
findings.quote: 'Noise reduction' compared mental health of people who lived in streets with different levels of traffic noise following introduction of a bypass, but no differences were found.

'Wythenshawe Regeneration' reported evidence from a single item outcome scale and identified decreases in quality of life for both intervention and control groups, with an intervention group reporting a greater loss of quality of life, SDID = -0.11 (-0.21 to 0.01).

Following adjustment for demographic and socioeconomic factors they found no change overall but reported subgroup analysis suggesting people with lower socioeconomic status (SES) experienced a decrease in life satisfaction compared to those in the control areas, while people with higher SES living in the intervened areas reported an improvement in quality of life compared to those in the control areas.
'DIY Streets' reported a small beneficial effect on quality of life (SDID 0.54 (95% CI -1.23 to 0.15))

'Street parks' found any positive effect of improving green infrastructure on social isolation/inclusion outcome: 'Street parks' increased supportive acts of neighbouring (SDID 0.68, 95% CI -1.11 to 0.25).

MMN Weak social ties, SDID 0.21 (95% CI -0.63 to 0.19).
MMN Neighbour annoyance, SDID -0.73 (95% CI -1.16 to -0.30).

synthesis_conclusions: There is very little robust public health evidence from intervention studies that changes to the built environment can improve mental health, quality of life, social isolation or inclusion.

The review identified a relatively large number of studies and some of them were of reasonable quality, however they found a very small or no effect of built environment on mental health and wellbeing.
Small positive effects on fear of crime, social isolation/inclusion and quality of life outcomes were found in studies with unfavourable assessments of risk of bias.
evidence_gaps: More robust study designs are needed.
Interdisciplinary research involving public health, planning and urban design experts is required.
Robust research needs to be embedded into major town planning decisions.
There is a dearth of studies looking at more modest changes to cities such as provision of footpaths, foot bridges, public lavatories, benches, etc.
Robust process evaluation is needed to understand intervention context and implementation.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Assessed using revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2.0) for RCTs and ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. Only 4 studies provided robust data (Well London RCT: low RoB; GSW Philadelphia, Greening Vacant Lots, District Approach: moderate RoB). The remaining 9 controlled before-and-after studies were rated 'serious' or 'critical' risk for 'bias due to confounding'. Longitudinal studies had 'serious' risk for 'Missing data' due to large numbers of people not returning questionnaires.
heterogeneity_sources: Interventions ranged from large-scale neighbourhood refurbishments to small 'do-it-yourself' parks.
Description of interventions was often unclear, especially for large urban regeneration projects.
Study designs varied (RCTs, controlled before-and-after, longitudinal cohorts, repeated cross-sectional surveys).
Data collection methods varied (routine panel surveys, postal questionnaires, face-to-face interviews).

moderators.effect: For urban regeneration (NDC) and quality of life, lower SES individuals experienced a decrease in life satisfaction, while higher SES individuals experienced an improvement.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Lower SES: decrease in life satisfaction. Higher SES: increase in life satisfaction.

limitations: Restricted search to publications written in English.
Focused on urban environments in high-income countries.
